title: SPMD vs MIMD Architecture in Distributed Computing
prompt: Explain the relationship between Flynn's MIMD classification and the Single Program, Multiple Data (SPMD) programming model used by MPI.
solutionSteps: Hardware Perspective: Cluster systems fall under MIMD (Multiple Instruction, Multiple Data) because each computing node has an independent CPU fetching its own instruction stream and operating on its own private memory.
Software Model: MPI enforces the SPMD (Single Program, Multiple Data) abstraction. A single compiled binary executable is distributed and executed across all nodes.

Execution Divergence: Although each process starts from the identical binary, processes differentiate their runtime execution paths using conditional branching on their unique process identifier: if (my_rank == 0) { ... } else { ... }.
watchOutTip: Do not confuse SPMD with SIMD. In SIMD (e.g. GPU vector units), execution units lock-step execute the exact same instruction simultaneously. In SPMD, processes execute asynchronously at independent clock speeds.

title: Communicators and MPI_COMM_WORLD
prompt: What is an MPI communicator? What two primary components constitute a communicator, and why is communicator caching/scoping essential in large software libraries?
solutionSteps: Definition: An MPI Communicator is an opaque handle (type MPI_Comm) representing a communication domain that encompasses a collection of processes.

Two Constituents: 1. A process group (an ordered set of process IDs with assigned ranks 0 to size-1). 2. A communication context (an internal unique tag space preventing message interference across distinct program modules).

Library Isolation: If a third-party linear algebra solver used raw ranks and tags on MPI_COMM_WORLD, its internal messages could collide with application messages having the same tag. Communicators (via MPI_Comm_dup or MPI_Comm_split) create isolated communication universes.

title: Eager vs Rendezvous Protocol in Blocking Communication
prompt: MPI_Send is described as 'blocking'. Does this guarantee that the destination process has actually received the message before MPI_Send returns? Explain using eager and rendezvous protocols.
solutionSteps: Strict MPI Standard Definition: A blocking send returns when the user's send buffer can be safely overwritten or reused without corrupting the message. It does NOT guarantee delivery to the receiver.
Eager Protocol (Small Messages): The runtime copies the message directly into an internal system buffer on the sender or network interface and returns immediately, before any MPI_Recv is posted.

Rendezvous Protocol (Large Messages): The sender transmits an envelope/handshake. The sender blocks until the destination posts a matching MPI_Recv and acknowledges readiness. Only then is payload data copied.
watchOutTip: Never rely on buffering! Code that succeeds for small test arrays can deadlock without warning on larger inputs when the MPI implementation transitions to the rendezvous protocol.

title: MPI_PROC_NULL Semantics and Utility
prompt: What is MPI_PROC_NULL and how does it simplify boundary conditions in ring and pipeline communications?
solutionSteps: Definition: MPI_PROC_NULL is a predefined constant rank recognized by all MPI point-to-point and collective routines.

Behavior: Any send directed to MPI_PROC_NULL returns immediately with success without transmitting data. Any receive from MPI_PROC_NULL returns immediately, leaving the buffer untouched and setting status.MPI_SOURCE = MPI_PROC_NULL.

Utility: Eliminates special-casing if statements at array boundaries. In odd-even sort or a 1D pipeline, Rank 0 can simply set left_neighbor = MPI_PROC_NULL and execute the exact same Sendrecv call as intermediate processes.

title: Collective Communication Rules and Tag Absence
prompt: Why do MPI collective communication routines (such as MPI_Bcast and MPI_Reduce) not include message tags? What are the three cardinal rules for invoking collectives?
solutionSteps: Absence of Tags: Collective routines match based strictly on the sequence of collective calls made on the communicator. Processors must execute collectives in the exact same program order, making tags redundant.
Rule 1: All processes in the specified communicator MUST call the collective routine.
Rule 2: Every process must supply matching arguments (e.g. identical root rank, identical operation operator).
Rule 3: Collective calls must not be enclosed in conditional branches where only a subset of ranks execute them (unless using a partitioned sub-communicator created with MPI_Comm_split).

title: Block vs Cyclic vs Block-Cyclic Decomposition Trade-offs
prompt: Compare Block, Cyclic, and Block-Cyclic distributions of a 1D array across P processes in terms of data locality and computational load balance for triangular matrix algorithms.
solutionSteps: Block Distribution: Process i receives contiguous slice [i*(N/P) .. (i+1)*(N/P)-1]. Excellent spatial locality and stride-1 cache access. However, for triangular matrices (where row length shrinks), high-rank processes finish early, leading to severe idle load imbalance.

Cyclic Distribution: Element k assigned to rank (k % P). Interleaves work evenly so all processors share both long and short rows in triangular systems. However, stride-P memory access destroys cache locality and requires fine-grained scatter/gather communication.

Block-Cyclic Distribution: Divides array into blocks of size B, distributing blocks cyclically. Yields the optimal compromise: maintains block spatial locality within cache lines while ensuring balanced load distribution across processes (foundation of ScaLAPACK).

title: Odd-Even Transposition Sort Phase Convergence
prompt: State the theorem governing the number of phases required to sort a distributed list of N keys across P processes using parallel odd-even transposition sort.
solutionSteps: Theorem: Given a distributed list of keys partitioned equally across P processes, after P phases of alternating even and odd pair exchanges, the entire list is globally sorted.
Local Step: Prior to phase 0, each process sorts its local block of N/P keys sequentially using qsort (cost O((N/P) log(N/P))).
Phase Step: In each phase, participating pairs execute a Compare-Split (Merge-Low / Merge-High) exchange using MPI_Sendrecv. After P phases, no element can be out of position.

title: Hadamard Product vs True Matrix Multiplication
prompt: Distinguish between Hadamard Matrix Multiplication and Standard Matrix-Matrix Multiplication in terms of mathematical definition, parallel decomposition, and communication overhead.
solutionSteps: Mathematical Definition: Hadamard product C = A o B is element-wise: C[i][j] = A[i][j] * B[i][j]. Standard matrix product C = A x B is row-by-column inner product: C[i][j] = sum_k (A[i][k] * B[k][j]).
Parallel Communication: Hadamard multiplication is embarrassingly parallel. If A and B have matching distributions, each process multiplies its local sub-matrix with ZERO inter-process communication.
True Matrix Product: Requires elements from row i of A to meet elements from column j of B across all processes, necessitating global broadcast/allgather or Cannon's 2D grid circular shifts.

title: Predict Output: MPI_Allreduce vs MPI_Reduce
prompt: Given 4 processes, each with local = rank * 10. Process 0 executes MPI_Reduce into total, and all processes execute MPI_Allreduce into all_total. Predict the printed values on Rank 2 and Rank 0.
solutionSteps: Step 1: Local values: R0=0, R1=10, R2=20, R3=30. Sum = 60.
Step 2: In MPI_Reduce(..., root=0), total on Rank 0 becomes 60. On Rank 2, total remains uninitialized (or 0).
Step 3: In MPI_Allreduce(...), all_total on EVERY process (including Rank 2 and Rank 0) becomes 60.
Step 4: Output for Rank 0: total=60, all_total=60. Output for Rank 2: all_total=60.

title: Predict Output: Ring with Rank Decrement
prompt: Assume np = 4. Rank 0 initializes token = 100. Each process receives from (rank-1+4)%4, subtracts its own rank, and sends to (rank+1)%4. What token value arrives back at Rank 0?
solutionSteps: Step 1: Rank 0 sends 100 to Rank 1. Then Rank 0 waits for message from Rank 3.
Step 2: Rank 1 receives 100, subtracts rank (1) -> token = 99. Sends 99 to Rank 2.
Step 3: Rank 2 receives 99, subtracts rank (2) -> token = 97. Sends 97 to Rank 3.
Step 4: Rank 3 receives 97, subtracts rank (3) -> token = 94. Sends 94 to Rank 0.
Step 5: Rank 0 receives 94.
expectedOutput: Token completed ring, received at Rank 0 = 94

title: Predict Output: MPI_Allgather Vector Reconstruction
prompt: 4 processes each hold 2 elements: Rank 0: [1, 2], Rank 1: [3, 4], Rank 2: [5, 6], Rank 3: [7, 8]. MPI_Allgather is called with sendcount=2, recvcount=2. What is in the receive buffer of Rank 3?
solutionSteps: Step 1: MPI_Allgather gathers 2 elements from each of the 4 processes and places the concatenated result on ALL processes.
Step 2: Total received elements on every process = 2 * 4 = 8 elements.
Step 3: Elements are stored in order of ascending rank.
Step 4: The receive buffer on Rank 3 (and all other ranks) is [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8].

title: Predict Output: Barrier Synchronization Effect
prompt: Consider two loops: loop 1 prints 'A <rank>' without barrier; loop 2 prints 'B <rank>' where rank 0 sleeps 1 sec before MPI_Barrier. Can 'B 0' print before 'A 3'?
solutionSteps: Step 1: Without a barrier between loop 1 and loop 2, fast processes can finish loop 1 and enter loop 2 before slow processes even start loop 1.
Step 2: However, if an MPI_Barrier separates phase A and phase B, NO process can enter phase B until ALL processes have exited phase A.
Step 3: Therefore, with an intervening barrier, 'B 0' can NEVER print before 'A 3'.
expectedOutput: With an intervening MPI_Barrier: No, all 'A' messages must complete across all ranks before any 'B' message can print.

title: Bug in Trapezoidal Function Return Type (Lecture Slide Mistake)
solutionSteps: Bug 1 (Return Type): Function is declared returning 'int' instead of 'double'. Returning int casts 'integral' to integer, truncating all fractional components and destroying numerical precision.
Bug 2 (Loop variable x): 'int x;' truncates grid evaluation points to integers (e.g. 0.5 becomes 0), evaluating f at completely incorrect abscissae.
Fix: Declare function as 'double Trap(double a, double b, int n, double h)' and declare 'double x;'.
watchOutTip: Watch out for this exact error in lecture slides! It is frequently tested in lab exams as a 'find the error and fix it' question.

title: Head-to-Head MPI_Send Deadlock
solutionSteps: Bug: Symmetrical send ordering. Both processes execute MPI_Send before posting MPI_Recv.
For small N, the MPI eager buffer absorbs the message. But for large N (1,000,000 ints = 4MB), MPI switches to the rendezvous protocol.
Rank 0 blocks waiting for Rank 1 to post MPI_Recv; Rank 1 blocks waiting for Rank 0. Neither can reach line 3. Circular dependency causes permanent deadlock.
Fix: Either invert order on Rank 1 (Rank 1 calls MPI_Recv first), or replace with MPI_Sendrecv.

title: Incorrect sendcount in MPI_Scatter
solutionSteps: Bug: sendcount argument in MPI_Scatter is specified as 16 instead of 4.
Rule: sendcount in MPI_Scatter denotes the number of elements sent to EACH individual process, NOT the total array count.
Passing 16 instructs MPI to send 16 elements to each of the 4 processes (requiring 64 elements in data). This causes a buffer overflow segmentation fault or MPI_ERR_TRUNCATE.
Fix: Change sendcount from 16 to 4 (or 16 / comm_sz).

title: Mismatched Collective Roots
solutionSteps: Bug: Collective root mismatch and conditional divergence.
Even ranks execute MPI_Bcast expecting root = 0; odd ranks execute MPI_Bcast expecting root = 1.

In MPI, all participating processes in the communicator must agree on identical root arguments for collective routines. Mismatched roots violate the specification and cause deadlocks or corrupt transfers.
Fix: All processes must call MPI_Bcast with the exact same root parameter (e.g. root = 0).

title: Buffer Truncation in MPI_Recv
solutionSteps: Bug: The receive buffer is smaller than the transmitted message payload (5 doubles vs 10 doubles).
In MPI, receiving fewer elements than were transmitted is a fatal truncation error (MPI_ERR_TRUNCATE). The MPI standard forbids truncating incoming messages without explicit configuration.
Fix: The receive buffer count in MPI_Recv must be greater than or equal to the sender's count (at least 10).
correctCode:
double arr[10];
MPI_Recv(arr, 10, MPI_DOUBLE, 0, 0, MPI_COMM_WORLD, MPI_STATUS_IGNORE);

title: Missing Address Operator in MPI_Init
solutionSteps: Bug: MPI_Init requires pointers to argc and argv: int MPI_Init(int *argc, char ***argv).
Passing 'argc' and 'argv' by value passes an integer and char** instead of int* and char***.
MPI modifies command-line arguments to strip out MPI-specific launcher flags (such as -np), which requires modifying the variables via pointers.
Fix: Pass address: MPI_Init(&argc, &argv);

title: Passing Receive Buffer in In-Place MPI_Reduce
code:
int sum = local_val;
MPI_Reduce(&sum, &sum, 1, MPI_INT, MPI_SUM, 0, MPI_COMM_WORLD);
solutionSteps: Bug: Passing the identical buffer pointer as both sendbuf and recvbuf without MPI_IN_PLACE.
Standard C MPI restricts overlapping memory buffers for sendbuf and recvbuf in collective routines (aliasing violation).
Fix: Use separate variables for local send and global receive, or use the MPI_IN_PLACE special constant on rank 0.

title: Partner Out-of-Bounds in Parallel Odd-Even Sort
code:
int partner = (phase % 2 == 0) ? (rank ^ 1) : ((rank % 2 == 1) ? rank + 1 : rank - 1);
MPI_Sendrecv(local, n, MPI_INT, partner, 0, temp, n, MPI_INT, partner, 0, MPI_COMM_WORLD, MPI_STATUS_IGNORE);
solutionSteps: Bug: In odd phases, when rank == 3 (an odd rank), rank + 1 evaluates to 4 (which is >= comm_sz). When rank == 0 (an even rank), rank - 1 evaluates to -1.
Calling MPI_Sendrecv with an invalid rank like 4 crashes MPI with an invalid rank error.
Fix: Check boundary conditions. When partner < 0 or partner >= comm_sz, assign partner = MPI_PROC_NULL (or skip communication).

title: Program: Barrier-Ordered Sequential Output
prompt: Write a complete C MPI program where all processes print 'Process <rank> of <size> reporting' in strict ascending numerical order (Rank 0 first, then Rank 1, ..., Rank size-1).
solutionSteps: Use a loop over all possible ranks from 0 to size - 1.
In each iteration i, only rank i calls printf followed by fflush(stdout).
Follow each iteration with MPI_Barrier(MPI_COMM_WORLD) so no process advances to iteration i+1 until rank i has completed printing.
expectedOutput:
Process 0 of 4 reporting
Process 1 of 4 reporting
Process 2 of 4 reporting
Process 3 of 4 reporting

prompt: Write a complete C MPI program implementing a ping-pong exchange between Rank 0 and Rank 1 up to a LIMIT of 10 exchanges. Rank 0 initiates ping; Rank 1 replies with pong. Print the counter at each exchange.
solutionSteps: Ensure program checks that comm_size >= 2.
Maintain an integer ping_pong_count initialized to 0.
Loop while ping_pong_count < LIMIT. Rank (ping_pong_count % 2) increments the count and sends to (rank + 1) % 2, while the other rank receives.
Print the rank and count at each reception.
expectedOutput:
Rank 0 sent ping_pong_count 1 to Rank 1
Rank 1 received ping_pong_count 1 from Rank 0
Rank 1 sent ping_pong_count 2 to Rank 0

...

title: Program: Ring Topology Token Passing
prompt: Write a complete C MPI program for a ring topology. Rank 0 initializes token = 10. Each process receives from (rank - 1 + size) % size, adds its own rank to the token, and sends to (rank + 1) % size. Rank 0 prints the final value.
solutionSteps: Compute neighbor ranks: next = (rank + 1) % size; prev = (rank - 1 + size) % size.
To prevent deadlock, Rank 0 sends the initial token first, then waits at the end to receive the completed token from prev.
All other processes (ranks 1 to size - 1) receive from prev, add rank, and send to next.
Rank 0 receives from prev, adds 0, and prints the result.
expectedOutput:
Rank 0 starting token with value 10
Rank 1 received token, added 1 -> now 11, forwarding to 2
Rank 2 received token, added 2 -> now 13, forwarding to 3
Rank 3 received token, added 3 -> now 16, forwarding to 0
Rank 0 received back completed token = 16

title: Program: Trapezoidal Rule with MPI_Reduce (Lab 9 Task 1)
prompt: Write a complete C MPI program to estimate the integral of f(x) = 2x + 3 from a = 0 to b = 2 using the composite trapezoidal rule with n = 1024 trapezoids. Use MPI_Reduce with root = MAX(rank) = comm_sz - 1.
solutionSteps: Analytical Solution: Integral of (2x + 3) dx from 0 to 2 is [x^2 + 3x]_0^2 = (4 + 6) - 0 = 10.0.
Local partition: h = (b - a) / n. Each rank gets local_n = n / comm_sz trapezoids. local_a = a + rank * local_n * h; local_b = local_a + local_n * h.
Compute local trapezoid sum using Trap(local_a, local_b, local_n, h).
Call MPI_Reduce to sum local integrals into total_integral on root = comm_sz - 1.
Root process prints the total integral and compares with exact value 10.0.

title: Program: Parallel Vector Addition using MPI_Scatter and MPI_Gather
prompt: Write a complete C MPI program that adds two vectors X and Y of size N = 8. Process 0 initializes vectors X and Y, scatters them to 4 processes using MPI_Scatter, each process computes Z[i] = X[i] + Y[i], and results are collected back on Process 0 with MPI_Gather.
solutionSteps: Define N = 8, comm_sz = 4, so local_n = 2.
Allocate local buffers local_X[2], local_Y[2], local_Z[2] on all processes.
Call MPI_Scatter for X and Y with sendcount = local_n, recvcount = local_n.
Each process performs local vector sum: local_Z[i] = local_X[i] + local_Y[i].
Call MPI_Gather to gather local_Z back into global Z on root = 0 and print.

title: Program: Parallel Odd-Even Transposition Sort (Lab 9 Task 2)
prompt: Write a complete C MPI program implementing Parallel Odd-Even Transposition sort for N = 16 elements on 4 processes using MPI_Sendrecv. Test with array A = [15, 29, 100, 23, -14, 45, 178, 192, 246, -118, 0, 7, 1, 10, 25, 34].
solutionSteps: Local count is N / 4 = 4 integers per process.
Scatter the 16 numbers from Rank 0 to all 4 processes.
Sort local array of 4 integers using qsort.
Execute a loop of comm_sz = 4 phases (even phase: pair with rank^1; odd phase: if (rank%2==1) partner=rank+1 else partner=rank-1). Check partner bounds against MPI_PROC_NULL.
Participating pairs use MPI_Sendrecv to exchange blocks. Rank with smaller rank executes Merge-Low; rank with larger rank executes Merge-High.
Gather sorted arrays back to Rank 0 and display.

title: Program: Row-Striped Matrix-Vector Multiplication
prompt: Write a complete C MPI program to compute y = A * x where A is an N x N matrix (N = 4) and x is an N-element vector. Matrix A is distributed by rows (one row per process) and vector x is broadcast to all processes with MPI_Bcast.
solutionSteps: Root process initializes matrix A[4][4] and vector x[4].
Broadcast vector x to all 4 processes with MPI_Bcast.
Scatter rows of A: Rank i receives row A[i] (4 elements) via MPI_Scatter.
Each rank computes dot product: local_y = sum(A[i][j] * x[j]).
Gather local_y results back to root with MPI_Gather and print vector y.

title: Program: Parallel Level-Synchronous BFS Traversal (Lab 10)
prompt: Write a C MPI program implementing level-synchronous Parallel BFS on a 4-node cycle graph (0-1-2-3-0). Root node is 0. Traversal frontier is shared across iterations using MPI_Allreduce.
solutionSteps: Maintain an array visited[4] and frontier[4] initialized to 0. On rank 0, visited[0]=1, frontier[0]=1.
Broadcast initial visited state to all processes.
Each process is assigned a subset of vertices (e.g. vertex = rank). In each BFS step, if process's vertex was in frontier, it finds all unvisited neighbors and marks them in local_next_frontier.
Call MPI_Allreduce with MPI_LOR to merge local frontiers into global next_frontier across all ranks.
Update visited array. Loop terminates when frontier is empty.
expectedOutput:
BFS Level 1 discovered vertices: 1 3 
BFS Level 2 discovered vertices: 2

prompt: Write a snippet using non-blocking MPI_Isend and MPI_Irecv to perform a safe two-way exchange of integer arrays between Rank 0 and Rank 1 without any chance of deadlock.

title: Amdahl's Law Speedup Calculation
prompt: A sequential seismic analysis program spends 85% of its execution time in parallelizable matrix operations and 15% in strictly sequential file I/O. Calculate the theoretical speedup achievable on 8 processors and the theoretical maximum speedup as N -> infinity.
solutionSteps: For N -> infinity: S_max = 1 / (1 - P) = 1 / 0.15 ≈ 6.67x.
Conclusion: Even with an infinite cluster, this program can never achieve greater than 6.67x speedup due to the 15% serial bottleneck.
expectedOutput:
Speedup on 8 cores = 3.90x
Maximum theoretical limit = 6.67x

title: Cannon's Algorithm Communication Cost Model
prompt: Derive the communication latency equation for Cannon's 2D Matrix Multiplication on a sqrt(p) x sqrt(p) mesh with communication startup time t_s and word transmission time t_w.
solutionSteps: Problem setup: Multiplying two n x n matrices on p processes. Each process holds sub-blocks of size (n / sqrt(p)) x (n / sqrt(p)), meaning each block contains n^2 / p elements.
Phase 1 (Initial Alignment): Maximum shift distance is sqrt(p) - 1 for both A (row shift) and B (column shift). This requires 2 * (sqrt(p) - 1) message exchanges.
Phase 2 (Multiply-Shift Loop): Exactly sqrt(p) iterations. Each iteration performs 1 shift left for A and 1 shift up for B (total sqrt(p) - 1 shifts during loop).
Total communication time formula: T_comm = 2 * (sqrt(p) - 1) * (t_s + t_w * (n^2 / p)).
Computation time: sqrt(p) * (2 * (n / sqrt(p))^3) = 2 * n^3 / p flops * t_comp.

title: Parallel Odd-Even Transposition Sort Time Complexity
prompt: Analyze the time complexity of parallel odd-even transposition sort for N keys across P processes.
solutionSteps: Initial Local Sort: Each process sorts N/P keys sequentially. Using qsort, cost is O((N/P) * log(N/P)).
Communication in Phase: Exactly P phases. In each phase, participating processes send and receive N/P keys: T_comm_phase = t_s + t_w * (N/P). Total comm across P phases = P * t_s + t_w * N.
Local Merge-Low / High in Phase: Merging two sorted lists of size N/P takes O(N/P) operations. Over P phases, total merge computation is P * O(N/P) = O(N).
Overall Time Complexity: T(N, P) = O((N/P) * log(N/P)) + O(N) + O(P * t_s + t_w * N).

title: Binary Tree Broadcast vs Linear Broadcast Complexity
prompt: Compare the theoretical communication time of a naive linear broadcast (Rank 0 sends to all ranks one by one) versus a binomial tree broadcast implemented in MPI_Bcast for message size m bytes across P processes.
solutionSteps: Naive Linear Broadcast: Root performs P - 1 point-to-point sends. Time T = (P - 1) * (t_s + t_w * m) = O(P * m).
Binomial Tree Broadcast: At step 1, Rank 0 sends to P/2. At step 2, both ranks send to their sub-trees. Tree depth is ceil(log2(P)).
Binomial Tree Time: T = ceil(log2(P)) * (t_s + t_w * m) = O(log(P) * m).
Comparison: For P = 1024, linear broadcast takes 1023 steps, whereas binomial tree broadcast completes in only 10 steps!

title: Isoefficiency and Scalability of Parallel Trapezoidal Rule
prompt: Calculate the speedup and parallel efficiency of the parallel trapezoidal rule assuming computation time per trapezoid is t_calc and MPI_Reduce takes O(log P * t_comm) for N trapezoids on P processes.
solutionSteps: Sequential Time: T_seq = N * t_calc.
Parallel Time: T_par = (N / P) * t_calc + c * log2(P) * t_comm.
Speedup: S = T_seq / T_par = (N * t_calc) / ((N / P) * t_calc + c * log2(P) * t_comm) = P / (1 + (c * P * log2(P) * t_comm) / (N * t_calc)).
Efficiency: E = S / P = 1 / (1 + (c * P * log2(P) * t_comm) / (N * t_calc)).
Scalability: To maintain constant efficiency as P increases, problem size N must grow in proportion to P * log(P).

title: 1D Column-wise Decomposition Cost Model (Part 5 Slide 8)
prompt: According to the course slides, what is the communication cost model for 1D column-wise decomposition of matrix multiplication C = A x B of size n x n across p processes?
solutionSteps: Setup: Matrix A and B partitioned such that each process owns a column strip of width n / p.
Data Dependency: To compute its local columns of C, each process needs access to the entire matrix A (or all rows).
All-to-All / Allgather: Processes must execute an Allgather to exchange column strips. Each process broadcasts its strip of size n^2 / p to all other (p - 1) processes.
Communication formula: T_comm = (p - 1) * t_s + t_w * (p - 1) * (n^2 / p) = (p - 1) * (t_s + t_w * n^2 / p).
Comparison with Cannon: 1D decomposition scales as O(p), whereas Cannon's 2D decomposition scales as O(sqrt(p)), making 2D vastly superior for large clusters.

title: Foster's PCAM Methodology Analysis for Odd-Even Sort
prompt: Walk through the four phases of Foster's Design Methodology (Partitioning, Communication, Agglomeration, Mapping) for parallel odd-even transposition sort.
solutionSteps: 1. Partitioning: Decompose list of N numbers into fine-grained tasks where each task is a single number and its adjacent comparisons.
2. Communication: Determine data flow: tasks need adjacent keys to perform compare-exchange.
3. Agglomeration: Group N fine-grained tasks into P large contiguous blocks of size N/P to minimize network message startups and leverage local cache sorting (qsort).
4. Mapping: Assign the P agglomerated blocks to P physical cluster nodes arranged in a linear array, matching communication partners (p-1 and p+1).

title: Parallel BFS Scalability Bottleneck in Scale-Free Graphs
prompt: Why does level-synchronous parallel BFS perform poorly on scale-free graphs (e.g. social networks with power-law degree distributions) compared to regular mesh graphs?
solutionSteps: Mesh Graphs: Have large graph diameter (many levels) and bounded vertex degrees. Frontier sizes remain moderate and load is evenly distributed.
Scale-Free Graphs: Have the 'small-world' property (tiny diameter, e.g. 4-6 levels) and high-degree hub vertices.
Bottleneck 1: Hub vertices cause massive communication hotspots and catastrophic load imbalance when expanded.
Bottleneck 2: Global synchronization barrier (MPI_Allreduce) is required at every level, creating high synchronization latency that dominates the few total levels.
